Interesting game with a cool, if a bit heavy-handed, social commentary narrative. The game consists of you sifting through text conversations, articles and phone call transcripts to connect the dots and stop a terror plot.

While the reporting system is selective about what you can include in reports, it is also pretty dumb so some stuff is best left out, making the game more engaging than just "click the thing". You also need to make some decisions in real time that will impact how the story unfolds. I love the mechanic of asynchronous information between you and your suppervisor.

Overall: if you like story-oriented games and want something new and interesting, this game is worth around 10-15 bucks.

The endings of the game illustrate a profound philosophical statement that is revealed through allegory.

Of the three endings, both condemning Delacroix or condemning Thought, ultimately, is short-sighted and misses the point. By condemning Delacroix, an individual is removed, however, the system remains largely intact and unchanged, which falls short of the motivation for condemning Delacroix in the first place. By condemning Thought, you've done your job, however, completely overlooked Orwell's dire short-comings.

In life, [b]the average person scarcely once considers themselves as the prime suspect[/b]. Why incriminate yourself when you can incriminate everyone and anyone else? This is the question that the third ending addresses. The answer is this: By incriminating everyone else, you have deluded yourself into believing that you were somehow left out of the picture. [spoiler]You weren't.[/spoiler]



"[b]T͖̟͚̘̻̼̓͛̌̃͆h̨̦̙͛̑e̴̹̝͖̤̅̑ ̵̟̱̹͍̬̹̲ͮ̈́̈́̀ͣŅ͎͎͍̪̠̟͕a͙̣͌̉̒̑̀͊͡t̜̠̑ͧ̐̒ͤͭi̗͖̝ͯ̍͊́̄́o̸͉͖͇͎ͯ̂̒̃n͓̝̜̄̍ͦ̂̈́̍ͩ͞[/b]" is an allegory for [b]You[/b].


In order to protect [b]Yourself[/b] and insure [b]Your[/b] survival, [b]You[/b] have co-opted reality in such a way that [b]You[/b] will blame everyone and anyone else for anything that is "evil", that is to say, anything that goes against [b]Your[/b] self agenda. The short-coming of this, is that your perspective will always be partial and distorted; you will never have the full picture. [spoiler]Because you're missing [b]You[/b].[/spoiler]



The short-comings of "[b]Ö̸̰̩͓̝́̉̂ͪͅr̲̟̙̒͆ͥ̃̔͑̂w͔̺̪̼͈̘̿̓͗͛̽̈́ē̮̉̓̃ͥ͡l̥͍̤̯ͯ́͂̑̈́̚ͅlͪ[/b]" is an allegory for [b]Your[/b] partial and self-biased perception.


In the third ending, by voluntarily choosing to incriminate [b]Yourself[/b], you have done the most difficult thing: To bridge the gap that was left as a result of self-biased perception. By doing so, Orwell's short-comings were revealed, and ultimately, genuine change was brought forth. [spoiler][b]You[/b] can do this too, in life, if you so choose to.[/spoiler]



The end of "[b]O̹͉̐̌̓̒͋r̷̰̩̣̽̉ͮ̇̾w̪̝͈͋͗ͧ̅ͥ̔ͮe̵͓͇̩͉̥̺̝ͥͣ̅̃̉ͭ̚l͖̗̻͎̏̽l̴̘̺͚͓[/b]" is an allegory for the end of this self-biased perception.

This is a truly amazing game. It really gets you thinking about mass surveillance. It's hardly impartial, but you get to see both the good and the bad aspects. If you have an interest in privacy, play this game. If you have never given it much thought, play this game. If you've ever said 'I have nothing to hide, it doesn't matter', play this game.

Pros:
- really gets you thinking about mass surveillance
- you control how the story unfolds based on what information you pass on to the government
- the story has some really great twists and surprises that I didn't see coming

Cons:
- Playing involves dragging and dropping pieces of information onto profiles of people you're investigating, but sometimes the drag and drop function is finicky, I occasionally had to retry multiple times to grab a piece of data. Not a big issue, but a minor annoyance.

A warning to achievement hunters: *do not* look at any 100% achievement guides before playing, they will ruin the story. You'll need 2 playthroughs anyway. Just play through normally the first time and you should be able to get all remaining achievements the second time.

Verdict: 10/10
